article.title: RE Foundations / 10B / When Weird Weather Strikes

sentences.text: Most of us know about hurricanes, droughts, and floods.
But from time to time, nature delivers a weather event that is really unusual.
One day in 2005, people in a small town in Serbia saw an unusual sight.
It was raining frogs!
Without any warning, they found their streets filling with the little jumping creatures.
“There were thousands of them,” one person told a local newspaper.
“I thought perhaps a plane carrying frogs had exploded,” said another.
Scientists believe a tornado passed over a lake and sucked up the frogs.
It then dropped them on the town, far away.
As if tornadoes aren’t dangerous enough, some can actually be made of fire.
When a wildfire reaches very high temperatures, it causes the air to heat up and then rise.
Cooler air moves quickly to replace the hot air.
This creates strong winds, which suck up the fire.
When this happens—like it did in 2014, in Denver, United States—a fire tornado is created.
A tornado like this can become 15 meters wide and grow as tall as a 40-story building.
In 1942, hundreds of thousand-year-old skeletons were found under the ice of Lake Roopkund in the Himalayas.
Many had holes in their skulls—but they weren’t hurt in any other way.
For years, the cause of their deaths was a mystery.
Today, scientists think they were killed by giant hailstones.
Hailstones are balls of ice that form when raindrops turn into ice.
The ice pieces increase in size until the wind cannot hold them up.
This results in hailstones falling to the ground, often at speeds of over 160 kilometers an hour.
For the unlucky people at Lake Roopkund, there was nowhere to run.

main_idea.text: While common weather events are well-known, nature occasionally produces truly unusual weather phenomena.

key_details.meaning: People are familiar with standard weather events like hurricanes and floods.
Sometimes, nature creates weather events that are highly unusual.

main_idea.text: In 2005, a tornado in Serbia picked up frogs from a lake and dropped them on a town, causing a bizarre 'frog rain'.

key_details.meaning: Thousands of frogs suddenly appeared on the streets of a small town.
Scientists explain that a tornado sucked the frogs up from a nearby lake.
The tornado dropped the frogs far away from their original location.

main_idea.text: Fire tornadoes are created when intense heat from wildfires causes strong winds to suck up the fire, forming massive, dangerous structures.

key_details.meaning: Wildfires heat the air, causing it to rise and be replaced by cooler air.
This movement of air creates strong winds that pull the fire upward.
These fire tornadoes can grow very large, up to 15 meters wide and 40 stories tall.

signals.text: As if tornadoes aren’t dangerous enough

main_idea.text: Scientists now believe that giant, fast-falling hailstones caused the mysterious deaths of ancient people found under the ice at Lake Roopkund.

key_details.meaning: Ancient skeletons with skull injuries were discovered under the ice in the Himalayas.
Scientists attribute the deaths to giant hailstones.
Hailstones can fall at speeds over 160 kilometers per hour.

sections.function: Introduces the concept of unusual weather events.

central_idea.text: Nature occasionally produces bizarre and dangerous weather events, such as frog rain, fire tornadoes, and giant hailstorms, which have surprising causes and effects.

inferences.claim: The people in the Serbian town were likely shocked and confused by the sudden appearance of thousands of frogs.

evidence.span: I thought perhaps a plane carrying frogs had exploded

inferences.knowledge_bridge: Understanding human reactions to unexpected, large-scale events.

inferences.claim: The ancient people at Lake Roopkund had no time to escape the hailstorm because it happened so quickly and the terrain was difficult.

evidence.span: speeds of over 160 kilometers an hour

inferences.knowledge_bridge: Connecting the speed of the hailstones to the lack of escape routes.
